title: The Trader Principle
summary: Give value for value. Do not seek the unearned.

lessons.title: Give value for value
lessons.objective: State the trader principle as an exchange in which each person gives a value and receives a value.

exercises.prompt: What does the trader principle tell a person to do?

choices.text: Give value for value
Take what is useful and offer nothing
Hand over values and expect nothing back
Wait until someone else supplies every need

feedback.note: The principle is an exchange. Each side gives a value in return for a value.

exercises.prompt: Match each side of a trade to what it does.

pairs.left: The person who offers a good
The person who pays for it

feedback.note: A trade has two offerings. One value is given for another value.

exercises.prompt: Complete the short form of the principle.

feedback.note: Both blanks name the same idea: what is given and what is received are values.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that names the exchange.

feedback.note: Giving and receiving are both part of the trade. Neither side is left out.

exercises.prompt: A mechanic fixes a car and the owner pays the agreed price. What is that, on this principle?

choices.text: Value given for value received
A loss, because money changed hands
A gift from the owner to the mechanic
A debt the mechanic still owes the owner

feedback.note: The repair is a value. The payment is a value. That is the exchange the principle names.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, what counts as the value in a trade?

choices.text: What one person offers the other in the exchange
A warm feeling with no offering
A title someone was born with
A wish that the other person will provide

feedback.note: A value here is something offered in exchange, such as goods, work, or payment.

exercises.prompt: Match each offering to the kind of value it is in a trade.

feedback.note: Goods, payment, and work can all be the values that change hands.

exercises.prompt: Finish the description of a trade.

parts.text: One person gives a value and

feedback.note: The second half of the exchange is receiving a value, not seizing one.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence states the trader principle?

choices.text: Give a value and take a value in return
Give only when you will get more than you give
Refuse every exchange
Let one person give and the other only take

feedback.note: The principle is two-sided. A value goes out and a value comes back.

lessons.title: Both sides gain
lessons.objective: Explain that a trade is an exchange in which each person gains a value, so neither is asked to lose for the other.

exercises.prompt: After a willing trade, who has gained a value?

choices.text: Each person in the exchange
Only the person who paid
Only the person who sold
Neither, because trade is a loss for both

feedback.note: Each side wanted what the other offered. Each leaves with a value.

exercises.prompt: Match each person in a sale to the gain.

pairs.right: Gets the good that was wanted
Gets the payment that was wanted
Is not a party to the gain

feedback.note: The gain belongs to the people who exchanged values, not to someone outside the trade.

exercises.prompt: Complete the claim about who gains.

feedback.note: The word each keeps both parties in the gain. A trade is not a win for only one side.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that rejects a one-sided loss.

feedback.note: Trade is not a demand that one person be worse off so the other can be better off.

exercises.prompt: A student pays a tutor for a lesson both agreed to. Which description fits?

choices.text: The student gains the lesson and the tutor gains the pay
Only the tutor gains, because knowledge was shared
Only the student gains, because money was spent
Both are harmed, because an exchange occurred

feedback.note: The lesson is a value to the student. The pay is a value to the tutor. Both gain.

exercises.prompt: Why is a trade not a sacrifice of one person to the other?

choices.text: Each person receives a value in return
Because one person must be hurt
Because nothing of value changes hands
Because a third person orders the deal

feedback.note: A sacrifice would be a loss with no value in return. A trade returns a value to each side.

exercises.prompt: Match each pattern to the result.

pairs.left: One side gives and gets nothing
One side takes and gives nothing

feedback.note: Only the two-way exchange leaves a gain on both sides.

exercises.prompt: Name what each trader walks away with.

feedback.note: The point of the exchange is a gain for each person who took part.

exercises.prompt: Two neighbors swap a spare chair for a spare lamp. Both wanted the swap. What does the principle say?

choices.text: Each gave a value and each gained a value
It fails, because no money was used
Only the person with the chair gained
One neighbor now owes a further unpaid gift

feedback.note: Money is one form of value, not the only one. A willing swap of goods is still value for value.

lessons.title: Do not seek the unearned
lessons.objective: Identify the unearned as a value one seeks without giving a value in return, and reject that aim.

exercises.prompt: What does this unit tell you not to seek?

choices.text: The unearned
Payment for work you did
A good you pay for
A skill you practice to learn

feedback.note: The second clause of the unit is a refusal: do not seek the unearned.

exercises.prompt: Match each aim to whether it seeks the unearned.

pairs.left: Pay for a coat you want
Demand the coat and offer nothing
Ask for praise you did not earn

feedback.note: The unearned is a value sought with no value given back, whether the value is a good or praise.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rule.

feedback.note: Unearned names what was not given in exchange and was not produced by the person who wants it.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that defines the thing to refuse.

feedback.note: Nothing given back is what makes the aim unearned. A return of value would make it a trade.

exercises.prompt: Someone wants a wage for a job that was never done. What is that want?

choices.text: Seeking the unearned
Ordinary pay for work performed
Value given for value
Practice that builds a skill

feedback.note: A wage is a value. Wanting it for work that was not done is seeking it unearned.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is earned, not unearned?

choices.text: A fee for a repair you actually made
Credit for a book you did not write
Goods taken and not paid for
Honor demanded for no achievement

feedback.note: The fee matches a value that was given. The other three seek a value with nothing offered.

exercises.prompt: Match each value to how a trader treats it.

pairs.left: Praise for a deed not done

feedback.note: Earned return is kept. Unearned goods and unearned praise are both refused.

exercises.prompt: Finish the contrast.

parts.text: and does not seek what is unearned.

feedback.note: Earned means a value tied to a value you gave. That is what the principle allows you to seek.

exercises.prompt: A neighbor offers you a birthday gift you did not demand. You may accept it. What would still break the principle?

choices.text: Treating further gifts as something you are owed
Thanking the neighbor for the gift
Keeping a gift that was freely offered
Later buying something from that neighbor

feedback.note: A free gift is not a claim. Seeking more as if it were owed is seeking the unearned.

exercises.prompt: Build the refusal in plain words.

feedback.note: The refusal is aimed at the unearned value, not at values you have actually earned.

lessons.title: Trade is not taking
lessons.objective: Tell a trade apart from taking, from a one-sided demand, and from payment that does not match a value given.

exercises.prompt: Which action is a trade?

choices.text: Buying a book at the price the seller asks
Walking off with the book and paying nothing
Ordering the seller to hand it over
Claiming the book because you want it

feedback.note: Buying gives a value for the book. Taking, ordering, and mere wanting do not.

exercises.prompt: Match each action to its name in this unit.

pairs.left: A demand that others supply you

feedback.note: Only the first action gives value for value. The other two seek a value without a return.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast.

parts.text: A trade returns a value. Taking returns

feedback.note: The difference is the return. Taking leaves the other person with nothing in exchange.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that separates trade from a demand.

feedback.note: Trade needs a value coming back. An unpaid demand does not offer one.

exercises.prompt: A shopkeeper is told to give away stock because the customer needs it and will not pay. What is that?

choices.text: A one-sided demand, not a trade
A fair trade, because need is a payment
A gain for both, with nothing returned
Payment the shopkeeper has earned

feedback.note: Need is not a value offered in exchange. Without a return, the demand is not a trade.

exercises.prompt: You do half the agreed work and want the full agreed pay, with no change in the deal. What is off?

choices.text: The pay does not match the value given
Nothing; any pay is value for value
Doing any work at all is seeking the unearned
Accepting pay is always taking

feedback.note: Value for value means the return matches what was given. The unpaid half is sought unearned.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to the judgment.

pairs.left: Full work for the agreed fee
No work, but the fee is still claimed

feedback.note: Matching values and accepted terms mark a trade. A claim without work, or goods taken, does not.

exercises.prompt: Finish the test for a real trade.

feedback.note: If nothing is given, there is nothing to call a trade, no matter how much is received.

exercises.prompt: Which pair is value for value?

choices.text: Ten hours of agreed work for the pay those hours earn
No hours of work for that same pay
A coat from a shelf and an empty hand
A prize for a contest you did not enter

feedback.note: The hours and the pay answer each other. The other pairs seek a value that was not given.

lessons.title: Both clauses together
lessons.objective: Hold the full rule: give value for value, and do not seek the unearned, including when a case looks mixed.

exercises.prompt: Which statement is the whole trader principle?

choices.text: Give value for value, and do not seek the unearned
Give value for value, and also take whatever else you can
Do not seek the unearned, and do not trade either
Give values away and never receive one

feedback.note: The unit has two clauses. Both are required: exchange values, and refuse the unearned.

exercises.prompt: Match each clause to the job it does.

feedback.note: One clause tells you how to deal. The other tells you what not to go after. Together they are the principle.

exercises.prompt: Fill both clauses.

feedback.note: The first blank completes the exchange. The second names what a trader does not seek.

exercises.prompt: Build the full rule in one line.

feedback.note: Dropping either half would shrink the principle. The line keeps the exchange and the refusal.

exercises.prompt: A writer sells a story for an agreed fee, then also demands a prize for a contest she skipped. What fits the principle?

choices.text: Keep the fee and drop the prize demand
Keep the fee and demand the prize too
Return the fee, because selling is wrong
Drop the fee and demand only the prize

feedback.note: The fee is value for value. The prize for a contest she skipped would be unearned.

exercises.prompt: Which mistake drops only the second clause?

choices.text: Trading fairly, then also grabbing an extra unpaid bonus
Refusing every exchange, paid or unpaid
Giving values away and receiving none
Neither trading nor seeking anything

feedback.note: The fair trade satisfies the first clause. The unpaid bonus breaks the refusal of the unearned.

exercises.prompt: Match each mixed case to the clause it breaks or keeps.

pairs.left: Paid work at the agreed rate
A bonus claimed for work not done
pairs.right: Breaks do not seek the unearned
Breaks both the exchange and the refusal

feedback.note: Use both clauses on a mixed case. One part can be a real trade while another part is unearned.

exercises.prompt: Say what a trader does with each kind of value.

feedback.note: Earning is the path the principle allows. The unearned is left alone.

exercises.prompt: A friend pays you for helping move furniture, as you both agreed. You do the work. What should you conclude?

choices.text: The pay is earned, so taking it fits both clauses
Any pay from a friend is unearned
You should also bill strangers who did not hire you
You must refuse the pay to stay a trader

feedback.note: The help was a value and the pay is the value returned. That is the principle, not a special ban on friends.
